summary: Presents example use cases for DDoS Open Threat Signaling (DOTS), which aims to let different DDoS mitigation systems interoperate. The use cases describe how DOTS components interact, how they collaborate and what typical information they exchange. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary:
When a website is flooded with junk traffic, it needs to call for help from the people who can block that traffic. Right now each defence product has its own private way of asking for help, so the call is slow and manual.

DOTS is a set of standard signalling messages for this. This RFC gives three example stories of who calls whom, so the message format can be designed.

questions: how does ddos signaling work between components
how does ddos mitigation coordination work
when should you call an upstream itp for ddos help
how do you use a third-party ddos service
when should you call an upstream transit provider for ddos help
subtitle: Example scenarios showing how organizations coordinate to stop a distributed denial-of-service attack.

tldr.problem: When a denial-of-service attack lands, the defence systems in an Internet provider, a cloud service and an enterprise are all separate products with their own signalling. They cannot talk to each other, so asking for help is slow and manual.
tldr.mechanism: DOTS, the DDoS Open Threat Signaling effort, defines standard ways for these systems to exchange requests, status updates and telemetry. This RFC gives three worked scenarios showing who signals whom and what they say.
tldr.outcome: The scenarios fed the requirements in RFC 8612 and the DOTS protocol specifications, RFC 8782 and RFC 8783. The RFC says the list of scenarios is not exhaustive and that more will appear as DOTS is adopted.

today: RFC 8903 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It gives sample use cases that fed the requirements in RFC 8612 and the design of the DOTS protocols in RFC 8782 and RFC 8783. The RFC states that the use cases are not exhaustive and that more are expected as DOTS is adopted and evolves.

sections.title: Why Defenders Need to Talk to Each Other
sections.content:
At the time of writing, distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) mitigation is built on siloed, proprietary signalling schemes, with vendor lock-in as a side effect. Configuring, provisioning, operating and activating a defence is a manual and often slow process. Running several defences at once adds both technical and organisational hurdles. That raises operational complexity, which in turn degrades the defences, because those defences depend on reacting quickly.

The DDoS Open Threat Signaling (DOTS) effort sets out to specify protocols that let different mitigation solutions work together, so that attacks are detected in the same way, mitigation is requested in the same way, and attacks are described in the same way.

Because the solutions from different vendors differ widely, the primary goal of DOTS is high-level interaction between them: detecting an attack, starting and stopping help, and asking for the status of a mitigation in progress.

This RFC supplies sample use cases. They fed the requirements in RFC 8612 and the design of the DOTS protocols in RFC 8782 and RFC 8783. The RFC is explicit that the list is not exhaustive and that further use cases are expected as DOTS is adopted.
sections.plainLanguage:
Each vendor's defence product talks to itself and to nobody else. So when an attack is too big for one defence to handle, the people who need to help have to be phoned by hand.

DOTS tries to make that call automatic and standard.

sections.title: The Roles the Scenarios Use
sections.content:
The RFC reuses the terminology of RFC 8612 and adds five terms of its own.

A DDoS Mitigation System (DMS) is the system that actually performs the mitigation. It may be a cluster of hardware or software, and it may include an orchestrator that decides to outsource some or all of the mitigation to another DMS.

DDoS mitigation is the action that DMS performs. A DDoS Mitigation Service is a service sold to a customer, usually with a service level agreement that has to be met; the provider of that service is the DDoS Mitigation Service Provider, and it is that provider's job to run a DMS good enough to meet the agreement.

An Internet Transit Provider (ITP) is the entity that delivers the traffic to a customer's network. That may be an Internet service provider (ISP) or an upstream entity that delivers the traffic to the ISP.
sections.plainLanguage:
The scenarios use four kinds of organisation: the network being attacked, the system that defends it, the company that sells the defending service, and the transit provider that carries the traffic.

Keeping these straight matters, because the same word, mitigation, covers both the action and the service around it.

sections.title: Asking a Transit Provider for Help
sections.content:
An enterprise network usually has an existing relationship with its transit provider. That provider already sits on the path of the enterprise's inbound and outbound traffic and already knows the parameters of the enterprise's WAN connection, which makes configuring a mitigation service easier.

The scenario in Section 3.1 is the first of two directions. The enterprise runs a DMS in front of its own Internet-facing properties, such as web servers, authoritative DNS servers and Voice over IP servers, and has contracted with its transit provider for mitigation when an attack threatens to overwhelm the WAN links. In the other direction, the transit provider notices that the enterprise is the source of an attack and asks the enterprise's DMS to stop it at the source. Both directions involve the same client and server interactions, so only the first is detailed, though the second is also in scope.

The enterprise's DMS is configured so that when inbound traffic exceeds 50 percent of the provisioned upstream WAN link capacity it asks the transit provider for help. The DMS acts as the DOTS client and the transit provider acts as the DOTS server, which is integrated with its own DMS.

The exchange has seven steps. The attack starts against the enterprise's resources. The enterprise DMS detects it, classifies it and begins mitigating. It then finds that its own capacity or capability is not enough, and sends a mitigation request through its DOTS client to one or more DOTS servers on the transit provider. The server decides whether it is configured to honour requests from that client, and if so it asks its own DMS to act. While the mitigation runs, the server sends regular status updates with mitigation statistics and related information. When the attack ends, or falls to a level the enterprise can handle, the server tells the client that it has subsided. The client then asks the server to terminate the mitigation, and the server confirms once it has ended.

The signalling may travel in band on the same WAN link as the attack, or out of band on a separate dedicated link, or over some other connectivity such as a third-party 4G network. A request may also be triggered by a network administrator who confirms it manually, in which case it may come from a web browser or a mobile application. Where the enterprise is multihomed across several transit providers, each provider can only mitigate the traffic it transits, so the enterprise has to coordinate the services for each link.
sections.plainLanguage:
The enterprise defends itself first. When the flood is bigger than its own link can take, it asks its transit provider to filter the traffic upstream, where there is more capacity.

The exchange has a clear shape: request help, get status updates, then ask for the help to be withdrawn once the attack is over.

sections.title: Asking a Third-Party Service for Help
sections.content:
This scenario differs from the previous one because the mitigation service is not provided by the transit provider. The attack traffic does not pass through the third-party provider unless the network is configured to send it there, which needs changes to the routing or to DNS. Because of that, it suits large enterprises and large data centres, though it is not limited to them.

A common pattern is that providers have relationships with each other, forming an overlay of mitigation systems. When a provider's own capacity runs out during an attack, it may delegate the mitigation to another provider.

The enterprise first signs an agreement with one or more third-party providers, covering how traffic will be redirected to them and how the cleaned traffic will be returned. Redirection usually means announcing the prefix with BGP or redirecting with DNS, and the traffic may be tunnelled back, for example with GRE. Those traffic steering mechanisms are outside DOTS, but they have to be arranged in advance, and in some contexts such a change could be detected and mistaken for an attack.

When the enterprise is under attack, or is close to its capacity, the DOTS client asks the third-party provider to divert the traffic and start mitigating. Ongoing attack and mitigation status may be exchanged the same way. When the attack stops or eases, the client asks the provider to terminate the mitigation.
sections.plainLanguage:
Some companies buy their defence from a third party that is not the company carrying their traffic. That means the traffic has to be redirected to the defender before it can be cleaned.

The redirection is arranged in advance, using routing or DNS changes. The RFC notes that such a change could itself look like an attack.

sections.title: Orchestrating Several Defences at Once
sections.content:
In the orchestration scenario, one or more telemetry systems or monitoring devices watch a network, which may be an ISP network, an enterprise network or a data centre. When one of them detects an attack, it alerts an orchestrator that coordinates the mitigation systems within that domain. The telemetry systems may pass along a preliminary analysis of what they saw.

The orchestrator weighs the information it receives and starts one or more mitigation strategies, choosing for example between the DMS inside the enterprise and one provided by the transit provider. Which system and which technique to use may depend on the type of attack, and a person may have to confirm the choice by hand. The mitigation itself may take several steps, such as reconfiguring the network or updating functions that are already running, and it may involve outside resources such as a transit provider or a third-party service provider.

Three separate conversations use DOTS here, and the roles swap each time. The telemetry systems talk to the orchestrator as clients, with the orchestrator as server. A network administrator talks to the orchestrator through a web interface backed by a DOTS client, again with the orchestrator as server. The orchestrator then talks to the mitigation systems as a client, with each of them as server.

The telemetry systems are configured so that when a measurement crosses a set level, their DOTS client sends a mitigation request to the orchestrator, optionally with hints about what triggered it. The hints matter, because something that looks like an attack to one telemetry system may not be an attack when seen from the wider view of the orchestrator. The orchestrator acknowledges the request, so that it is not sent again, and may then collect finer information from other telemetry systems to correlate the measurements.

The orchestrator may be configured to start a mitigation only after a network administrator approves it, and it reports its analysis to that administrator, who then triggers the mitigation through a DOTS client. The orchestrator evaluates the volume of the attack and the value of the target, may pick a service provider according to the severity, and may also coordinate other work such as moving the target to another network so that new sessions are not affected. It then asks the chosen systems to mitigate, as in Section 3.1, and reports back that the mitigation is effective.

The reverse direction also exists. A mitigation system that reaches its own maximum capacity can send a request back to the orchestrator, known as offloading, with hints such as the traffic it has blocked. The orchestrator can then act further, for example by asking forwarding nodes such as routers to filter the traffic. Here the mitigation system is the DOTS client and the orchestrator the server. Configuring the mitigation systems, and discovering what functions they offer, are both outside DOTS.
sections.plainLanguage:
A large network may run several monitoring tools and several defence systems at once. An orchestrator sits between them, gathers what the monitors saw, and decides which defence to use.

Under pressure, a defence system can also ask the orchestrator for more help, in case the attack outgrows what it can filter.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document describes no protocol, but it does set out a few high-level security points. DOTS is at risk from three primary attacks: impersonation of a DOTS agent, injection of traffic, and blocking of the signalling.

Impersonation and traffic injection are addressed by ordinary secure communication practice, including mutual authentication. Loss of keepalive traffic can be partly handled by preconfiguring what happens when keepalives stop. Against an attacker who can selectively block any or all traffic, though, no comprehensive defence is possible. Using a different communication path that the attacker may not be able to block is another possible measure.

The detailed security requirements for DOTS are in RFC 8612. Service disruption may still be experienced if inadequate mitigation actions are applied, and the RFC leaves that out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage:
The signalling itself becomes a target. An attacker could pretend to be a defender, feed false information into the system, or simply block the messages that ask for help.

Mutual authentication handles the first two. The third cannot be fully solved, so the RFC suggests using a second path for the signalling.
